To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

group identification and boundary permeability interact in their effects on preferences for exit, loyalty, and collective action among workers in a simulated business environment, with the highest levels of loyalty and collective action being found for highly identified workers in low permeability conditions.

(1) when the group boundary is open, people who identify strongly with their group tend to remain loyal to their group and to choose collective action, and (2) people who identify weakly with their group tend not to remain loyal to the group when the boundary is open.

(1) when group members are more strongly identified with their in-group, they will be more loyal and less willing to exit, even under conditions in which there are opportunities to exit; and (2) when group members perceive that there are opportunities for exit, they will be less willing to engage in collective action, even if they are strongly identified with their group.

group identification and boundary permeability are both important factors in predicting exit from and loyalty to a group.
when options for mobility exist, group loyalty is more likely when group members are highly identified with their group.
